The city I live in has set up a special fixture for Gay Pride Week for the first time ever. Some residents are saying it's a breath of fresh air, while others want it gone. While I have no problem with the fixture being there, my issue come with the fact that they are using public funds to build and maintain this fixture.

I have been at odds with the city for quite some time now due to the civic sponsorship of a nativity scene in one of our main parks, and while doing some thinking, my original support for the Pride Week fixture started to seem a little hypocritical.

Is building a Pride Week fixture showing favoritism like the way setting up a Nativity scene at Christmastime would be, or is this more akin to the ceremonies and fixtures surrounding Veteran's Day?
Would using public funds for a fixture for Gay Pride Week be as objectionable as a public-funded religious fixture around Christmastime?
I don't think they should do either. Beyond anything else, why should a local government be spending money on stuff like that at all? Just let the groups involved build them if they want to.

To play devil's advocate... Don't both groups contribute funds to the public coffers (e.g. rates etc.)? If we accept that the city council is responsible for providing attractions that enrich the lives of its citizens (parks, libraries, etc.), and if we accept that only a subgroup of the population will make use of any of those amenities, how is it wrong to spend money to cater to Christian or homosexual demographics?

Don't both groups contribute funds to the public coffers

Sure, like everyone else. That doesn't mean the city has to create specific special needs projects for every possible demographic group that is forced to contribute.

If we accept that the city council is responsible for providing attractions that enrich the lives of its citizens (parks, libraries, etc.), and if we accept that only a subgroup of the population will make use of any of those amenities, how is it wrong to spend money to cater to Christian or homosexual demographics?

I don't accept any of that, but it's no more wrong than anything else the city does, it's just not necessary.

Our city started a gay pride week thing. It wasn't paid for by city funds, but I can tell you that it probably generated about $50,000 worth of business and brought in tourists that otherwise would not be familiar with the city. There is a direct economic benefit seen from the event. To me, if the city contributed $500 towards the event in the form of free police officers and no charge to shut down a small section of road, that's totally a reasonable investment in the event and they see a direct benefit from that investment.
If it's not paid for by city funds then there's no issue, but that's not what the OP is talking about.

I think my point was pretty clear that if the city contributes a small portion to an event that contributes to tourism and community lifestyle then I don't consider it a problem. But, yes, what you said is both true and painfully obvious.
